childhoodeyebrainimages.visual_development_intro_paragraph_1: When babies are born their vision is poor. They are essentially 'blind'. Their vision will however develop over the following 5 to 8 years with most improvement occurring in the first 18 months of life. This is a very critical period.
childhoodeyebrainimages.visual_development_intro_paragraph_2: During this time the visual system of the eyes and brain needs to be healthy and stimulated. This is the best period to identify disease and refer for treatment.
childhoodeyebrainimages.visual_development_brain_image_alt: The eyes and their visual connections to the brain
childhoodeyebrainimages.visual_development_identify_disease_titl: Why and how we identify disease to maximise visual development
childhoodeyebrainimages.visual_development_identify_disease_body: Any disease of the eye or brain will slow development and limit long term vision. This is why it is important to identify as early as possible any treatable causes of disease that is affecting normal visual and general development.
childhoodeyebrainimages.visual_development_question_bubble: This can be done by asking questions about vision, pregnancy, birth, any illnesses and general development
childhoodeyebrainimages.visual_development_observe_copy: then observe the eyes assessing visual development then screen for eye disease by performing the fundal 'red' reflex test and examining the front of the eye
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_1_paragr: Inside the womb, the unborn baby is surrounded by gentle and calming sound, including their mother's heartbeat and voices and sounds from the world outside.
As pregnancy reaches its final stages, the baby's eyes can open inside the womb.
While they can't yet see images or details, they can sense changes in light.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_1_image_: Pregnancy stage illustration of the unborn baby in the womb
Late pregnancy stage illustration showing awareness of light
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_2_paragr: At birth vision is very unlike that of an adult. A newborn is 'blind' with poor visual acuity of around 6/600. They do not perceive much colour and have low contrast sensitivity. They have no stereovision and their eyes may squint now and again.

They will however look directly at faces at very close range, and squeeze their eyes shut to bright lights. Their vision from now is going to develop very rapidly and become like an adult by 8 years of age.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_3_paragr: Within two weeks vision has improved hugely. They can now see some detail, especially if things are up close. There is no colour and what they do see is flat, because their eyes are not yet always straight and working together for depth perception.
Sometimes their eyes will drift in or out for a short while. This is called squinting. This should stop happening by three months.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_4_paragr: By one month colour vision is starting to develop. They will be much more visually interested especially to faces. They will also start to try to follow things that are moving.
They will become more and more aware of familiar sounds including well known voices like their family. And start to join up what they hear with what they see.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_4_image_: Visual development between two weeks and one month
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_5_paragr: By three months their eyes should always be straight and working together to create 3D vision. This new depth perception helps them reach for things more accurately. They will be able to follow things that are moving faster but it is hard to switch fixation from one face or object to another quickly.
They like to look at only one thing at a time. They may also start to make their first meaningful sounds.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_5_image_: Visual development between one and three months
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_6_paragr: An infant with normally developing vision will become excited at seeing a drinking cup or spoon and can routinely fix and follow a face at a distance of 1-2 metres as well as be able to differentiate between familiar and unfamiliar faces by both their faces and voices.
They can also start to see things that are further away. Driven by curiosity, they will begin to reach for things.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_7_paragr: At 6 to 12 months of age the visual acuity is improving and is around 6/36. The distance at which faces are looked at and recognised has extended to 2 metres. All elements of vision are improving with more accurate reach and grasp.

At this age they are becoming more interested in images in books and on television, although real objects are more engaging encouraging them to crawl and around their first birthday, walk towards objects of interest. Their babblings are developing, and sounds will become first words at this age as well.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_8_paragr: By 18 months, vision is quite adult like although still a bit blurry at visual acuity of around 6/18. They will now be able to recognise their name and be using more and more words.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_8_image_: Visual development between twelve and eighteen months
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_9_paragr: After 18 months of age vision still needs several years to mature. Normal adult visual acuity will be formed by the age of 8.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_9_image_: Visual development between eighteen months and eight years
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_10_parag: After the age of 8 the visual system may not improve well to treatment such as cataract surgery. Identification of disease and referral for treatment is therefore best done as early in life as possible.

It can be seen that a huge amount of development occurs between birth and 18 months of age and continues more slowly throughout the rest of childhood. During this period it is essential that the child is healthy with a disease free visual system and provided with a stimulating and educationally nourishing environment.
Early identification of disease with referral for treatment is important to help maximise both visual and general development.
